Method-Application Synergies: Population models of bacterium-phage relationships were used to examine the role of latent phage in bacterial populations over time in response to antibiotic treatment.
Mathematical modeling was applied to understand the impact of antibiotics on the bacterium-phage system with multiple phage strategies and antibiotic resistance.
Dynamical systems modeling was used to simulate population dynamics of bacteria and phages under various antibiotic administration scenarios.
Complementary Technique Synergies: The collaboration combined biological understanding of bacterial infections and phage lifestyles with mathematical modeling techniques to predict outcomes.
Sensitivity analyses using Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) and partial rank correlation coefficients (PRCC) were applied to the biological model parameters.
Data-Method Synergies: Model parameters were selected based on existing biological literature and experimental estimates for P. aeruginosa and phages.
The model's predictions on bacterial population control were compared with clinical evidence from cystic fibrosis patients treated with antibiotics.
Cross-Domain Fusion Topics: Modeling the control of bacterial infections via antibiotic-induced proviruses.
Phage-antibiotic synergy in the context of temperate and chronic viruses persisting in latent form.
Personalized medicine approaches based on identification of latent viruses in bacterial strains for antibiotic stewardship.
Shared Application Areas: Management of common bacterial infections, particularly Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Strategies for antibiotic stewardship and personalized medicine approaches.
Understanding and controlling antibiotic resistance in clinical settings.
Joint Technique Development: Development of a population model incorporating two competing bacteriophage types (temperate and chronic) and antibiotic stress.
Incorporation of nonlinear infection rates (Michaelis-Menten or Hollings type II functional response) and stress-dependent phage production/cell reproduction functions.
Theory-Application Synergy: Mathematical models of bacterium-phage systems, including logistic growth and functional responses, were applied to understand antibiotic treatment outcomes.
The theoretical framework demonstrated how antibiotic-induced phage lysis could control bacterial infections, even with antibiotic resistance.
Thinking Pattern Synergies: Biological insights into phage lifestyles and antibiotic mechanisms informed the structure and parameters of the mathematical model.
Mathematical analysis of the model provided quantitative predictions and sensitivity analyses to guide biological understanding and potential treatment strategies.
Future Research Directions: Investigating the impact of cross-resistance to phage infection on phage-antibiotic synergy.
Incorporating density-dependent latency probability for phages that detect bacterial population density.
Integrating evolutionary dynamics into the model to explain longer-term dynamics in chronic infections.
Experimentally measuring the relative number of bacteria killed by direct antibiotic action versus phage induction.
Summary Collaboration Themes: This collaboration fused microbiology and mathematics to model the control of bacterial infections, specifically P. aeruginosa, through antibiotic-induced proviruses. By developing a population model that integrated temperate and chronic phage lifestyles with antibiotic stress, they demonstrated how antibiotics can be effective even against resistant bacteria by triggering phage induction. This work expands understanding of phage-antibiotic synergy and suggests personalized medicine approaches for antibiotic stewardship.
